title: Evaluating the Short-Form Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale in a Japanese university EFL context: internal-structure evidence and score-interpretation boundaries
text_snippet: Evaluating the Short-Form Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale in a Japanese university EFL context: internal-structure evidence and score-interpretation boundaries Abstract Foreign language classroom anxiety remains a central construct in applied linguistics, but brief instruments require context-specific evidence before their scores are used for substantive interpretation. This study examined the eight-item Short-Form Foreign Language Classroom Anxiety Scale (S-FLCAS) with 826 Japanese university learners of English as a foreign language. The study provides internal-structure and item-functioning evidence for a provisional, low-stakes interpretation rather than a complete validation or formal replication. Ordinal confirmatory factor analysis supported a dominant one-factor structure, and reliability was acceptable for a brief scale (α = 0.84; ω = 0.84). Rasch partial-credit modeling showed ordered response thresholds, interpretable item-intensity differences, and mostly acceptable item fit. Content comparison with the full FLCAS suggests that the short form emphasizes a narrower classroom-speaking and evaluative-pressure core. Separately, CFA and Rasch residual diagnostics showed localized dependence for Items 1–2 and Items 6–7. title: Authenticity of academic lecture passages in high-stakes English tests: interrelations among temporal fluency features
text_snippet: Authenticity of academic lecture passages in high-stakes English tests: interrelations among temporal fluency features Abstract In listening assessment, a domain definition inference of temporal fluency features remains under-researched, posing a challenge for test developers in creating authentic listening texts. To address this issue, this paper reports two studies. Study I examined interrelations of temporal fluency features (e.g., articulation rate) in lecture settings. Lecture passages in TOEFL iBT and IELTS were compared to real-world data (Fluency Corpus of Academic English Lectures [FCAEL]). Results showed both similarities (e.g., positive association between articulation rate and end-clause silent pause frequency), and dissimilarities (e.g., correlations between articulation rate and mid-clause filled pause frequency and between repetition frequency and mid-clause filled pause frequency) among the three. Since correlations do not necessarily indicate that disfluencies co-occur, Study II investigated co-occurrences of two disfluency features that indicated high correlations in Study I (i.e., repetitions and filled pauses) in FCAEL and TOEFL. title: How the Konkur, principals, and parents shape novice EFL teachers’ classroom assessment in Iran?
text_snippet: How the Konkur, principals, and parents shape novice EFL teachers’ classroom assessment in Iran? Abstract This sequential explanatory mixed-methods study investigates the classroom assessment realities of novice EFL teachers in Iran’s public secondary schools—a context defined by large classes, limited resources, and the pervasive washback of the Konkur (university entrance examination). Drawing on Xu and Brown’s (2016) Teacher Assessment Literacy in Practice (TALiP) framework, the study integrates survey data ( N = 158), semi-structured interviews ( n = 20), and document analysis ( n = 18 tests) to address three questions: the challenges teachers face in constructing classroom achievement tests; how teachers navigate between assessment principles from pre-service education and daily practical demands; and what supports teachers identify as critical for their development relative to current availability. Findings document a constrained assessment ecology where time scarcity (M = 4.62) was the most strongly endorsed challenge, and a triad of stakeholder accountability pressures—Konkur expectations, principal oversight, and parental demands—was consistently associated with assessment decisions. title: Morphological awareness in TOEIC word-form questions: an item-type analysis of EFL learners’ performance and perceptions
text_snippet: Morphological awareness in TOEIC word-form questions: an item-type analysis of EFL learners’ performance and perceptions Abstract This study investigates Korean EFL learners’ performance on TOEIC-style word-form items from the perspective of morphological competence. Although morphological awareness has been widely discussed in relation to second language reading and vocabulary development, less attention has been paid to how learners handle different morphological item types in standardized grammar and vocabulary tasks. To address this gap, 277 Korean university students completed a 30-item TOEIC-style word-form test covering five item types: nouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, and participial/comparative forms. The study also examined the association between test performance and learners’ global perceived reading confidence. A repeated-measures analysis showed that accuracy varied across morphological item types. Noun and verb items showed relatively higher accuracy, whereas participial/comparative items showed comparatively lower accuracy than the other categories. In addition, perceived reading confidence was modestly but positively associated with overall test performance. title: The critical extension framework: making organisational assumptions explicit in multilingual writing assessment
text_snippet: The critical extension framework: making organisational assumptions explicit in multilingual writing assessment Abstract At the construct-articulation stage, current ESL writing rubrics quietly pull rhetorical preference into the operational definition of language proficiency. The interpretive consequences reach beyond measurement alone: once scores cannot tell organisational strategy apart from language control, teacher interpretation, feedback, and gatekeeping decisions all lose precision. This framework-development study traces the problem through critical discourse analysis of four major frameworks (TOEFL iBT, IELTS Academic Writing, CEFR, and classroom assessment principles). It shows how descriptor language governing organisation, coherence, and development encodes linear, thesis-first norms. Coding-scheme stability is established through intra-analyst (Cohen’s κ = 1.00) and inter-analyst (81.7 per cent agreement) checks on stratified subsets matched in size and scheme (12 of 34; 35.3 per cent). title: EFL teachers’ language assessment literacy training needs: the role of individual and contextual factors
text_snippet: EFL teachers’ language assessment literacy training needs: the role of individual and contextual factors Abstract Glocalization has become increasingly influential in language testing, by adopting and reshaping global assessment standards within the local educational context. One important area where this global and local interface unfolds is teachers’ language assessment literacy (LAL). This study examines how individual and contextual factors relate to in-service English as a foreign language (EFL) teachers’ LAL training needs in Yemen. Quantitative data were collected using the validated language assessment literacy questionnaire (LALQ) and analyzed using SPSS. The sample consisted of 471 Yemeni in-service EFL teachers teaching Grades 7 to 9. The findings reveal that teachers’ LAL training needs are not uniformly shaped by individual characteristics, including gender, educational qualifications, or years of teaching experience. Instead, these needs are strongly differentiated by contextual factors and professional development and by specific LAL dimensions rather than by overall assessment competence. title: Who acts, who watches: managing environmental responsibility in IELTS academic reading texts
text_snippet: Who acts, who watches: managing environmental responsibility in IELTS academic reading texts Abstract Environmental themes are increasingly visible in IELTS Academic Reading, yet less attention has been paid to how assessment texts organise ecological responsibility at the point where problem–solution narratives move toward closure. This study examines IELTS Academic Reading texts published between 2016 and 2023, with selected ELT materials included for analytic triangulation. Adopting a qualitative, mechanism-oriented discourse-analytic design, the analysis traces how environmental issues are staged and resolved through a sequential analytic chain combining Situation–Problem–Response–Evaluation (SPRE) staging, appraisal-informed mapping of evaluation, and critical diagnostics of agency and modality. Across the dataset, three recurrent closure-related patterns are identified: (1) ecosophical narrowing, in which late-stage evaluation shifts toward feasibility and instrumental benefit; (2) managerial response bias, which privileges expert-led, procedural, or technical interventions; and (3) evaluation without agency, in which optimistic closure is achieved through possibility-oriented modality and agent-backgrounding rather than obligation. title: Scanning techniques in EFL reading: a cross‑cultural study through the IELTS context
text_snippet: Scanning techniques in EFL reading: a cross‑cultural study through the IELTS context Abstract Mastering scanning techniques is essential for proficient EFL reading, particularly for learners preparing for proficiency tests such as IELTS. Yet, empirical validation of practical scanning strategies remains limited. This study examines the choices and preferences of scanning techniques among independent and proficient EFL learners from diverse linguistic and cultural contexts. A cross‑sectional design was employed with 173 Iranian and Hungarian participants. Three IELTS academic reading tasks were designed to test participants’ ability to locate four types of information: proper nouns, numerals, long phrases, and unfamiliar words, commonly encountered in actual IELTS tests. Prior to the tasks, learners were introduced to seven scanning techniques drawn from two IELTS textbooks. Results showed that Hungarians outpaced Iranians in completing the tasks, with certain techniques emerging as both efficient and frequent. Hungarians primarily favoured left‑to‑right eye movement, consistent with the directionality of their language, whereas Iranian learners exhibited more varied scanning patterns, with only modest tendencies toward right‑to-left techniques. title: Transformative learning in teacher development: the impact of a teacher education course on EFL teachers’ perceptions and experiences of the emotional dimensions of language assessment literacy
text_snippet: Transformative learning in teacher development: the impact of a teacher education course on EFL teachers’ perceptions and experiences of the emotional dimensions of language assessment literacy Abstract Although there is a surge of scholarly attention into language assessment literacy, emotions in language assessment literacy (ELAL) is a relative novelty in the field. The current study developed an ELAL-informed teacher education course to examine Iranian English as a Foreign Language (EFL) teachers' perceptions of ELAL and the course's impact. Data were collected from 32 teachers who completed a pre-post test questionnaire, as well as from 15 teachers who participated in semi-structured interviews and audio diaries. The course's effectiveness in improving teachers' perceptions, knowledge, and competencies was confirmed by significant increases in their ELAL scores from pre-test to post-test. Furthermore, the qualitative findings indicated that the participants were emotionally aware and made context-dependent modifications to practice. Importantly, the study identified ongoing tensions in the delicate balance between empathy and fairness, exposing the concealed emotional labor of assessment.
